userPrompt: Can a company in the EU refuse to give an employee their statutory annual leave?
responseText:
**No, a company in the EU cannot lawfully refuse to grant an employee their statutory minimum annual leave.**

### Key rules under EU law
- **Directive 2003/88/EC** (Working Time Directive) requires **at least 4 weeks (20 working days)** of paid annual leave per year for all workers. This is a mandatory health-and-safety right and cannot be waived by contract or agreement.
- Member States may set higher minimums (e.g. 25–30 days in many countries), but never lower than 4 weeks.
- The employer **must** allow the employee to actually take the leave. It is not enough to pay out the entitlement or carry it over indefinitely.

### What an employer can and cannot do
| Action                              | Lawful? | Notes |
|-------------------------------------|---------|-------|
| Refuse to let the employee take the statutory minimum leave | No | Direct breach of the Directive |
| Force the employee to work during scheduled leave | No | Except in genuine emergencies with proper compensation |
| Pay out unused leave instead of granting time off | Generally No | Only allowed on termination of employment |
| Carry over leave to the next year | Limited | Only for the part above the 4-week minimum, and usually only with agreement and for a limited time |
| Refuse reasonable requests for specific dates | Sometimes | Employer can refuse for “compelling business reasons” but must still ensure the full entitlement is taken within the legal timeframe |

### Practical consequences of refusal
- The employee can file a claim before a labour court or authority.
- In most Member States this is treated as a serious breach; the employee can often force the taking of leave plus claim compensation or damages.
- Persistent refusal can also be challenged as a health-and-safety violation.

**Bottom line**: Statutory annual leave is not a discretionary benefit. An EU employer must ensure the employee receives and can actually take at least the 4-week minimum (or the higher national minimum). Refusing it outright is illegal.
